sample_unit: expert assessments (5 EM faculty x 10 questions x 8 domains per chatbot; 400 per chatbot)

links.outcome: Recognition and appropriate advice for emergency conditions; dangerous information in chatbot responses
links.effect: Chatbots contained dangerous information in 5% to 35% of responses; accuracy and completeness about 50%; information on when to seek urgent care frequently incomplete and inaccurate.
links.quote: Chatbots contained dangerous information in 5% to 35% of responses, with no statistical difference between chatbots on this metric (P=.24).

links.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading level of chatbot responses relative to emergency patients
links.effect: Reading level was 7.7-8.9 grade for all chatbots except ChatGPT at 10.8, all too advanced for average emergency patients.
links.quote: Flesch-Kincaid Reading level was 7.7-8.9 grade for all chatbots, except ChatGPT at 10.8, which were all too advanced for average emergency patients.

links.outcome: Source reliability and relevance of citations in chatbot responses
links.effect: Source relevance and reliability performance was poor (10%), sources mostly unreported; Bing AI 40% identified or relevant sources, others 0%-10%.
links.quote: Only Bing AI performed better with more identified or relevant sources (40%; the others had 0%-10%).

screen.reason: Evaluated the accuracy, safety, and readability of four commercial LLM chatbots in answering emergency care patient queries, but did not test a specific deployment safeguard or practice.
